fields.definition: The specific situation you want to change, described from the point of view of the people affected. A good problem statement says who is affected, where, how much, and why it happens. It does not mention your organisation or what you plan to do.
fields.strongExample: In a rural district, nearly 4 in 10 girls who start secondary school leave before finishing lower secondary, compared with 2 in 10 boys. Families point to the cost of fees, uniforms and transport. Girls describe the long walk to school as unsafe, and many take on more household work as they get older.

weakExample.text: There is a lack of scholarships for girls in our area.
weakExample.whatIsWrong: This describes a missing solution, not the problem. It assumes scholarships are the answer before looking at why girls leave school, and it says nothing about who is affected or how many.
weakExample.improved: Girls in our district leave secondary school earlier than boys. Cost is one of several reasons families give, alongside safety and household work.

fields.tip: Keep it to one or two sentences and narrow it down to a group, a place or one part of a bigger issue. Asking 'why does this happen?' several times helps you move from symptoms to causes, but check your answers against data and against what the people affected tell you.

sources.title: Theory of change in ten steps

fields.definition: The main things your team will do, using your staff, money and materials, to produce your outputs. Activities are actions, so they start with a verb such as train, run, distribute or organise. Describe them specifically enough that someone could plan and budget them.
fields.strongExample: At the start of each term, assess the reading level of every pupil in Years 3 to 5 in 20 schools. Group pupils by reading level rather than by year for one hour a day, using simple materials matched to each level. Give each teacher a mentor who visits monthly to observe and support.

weakExample.text: Improve children's reading through innovative education approaches.
weakExample.whatIsWrong: This is a result you hope for, not something your team does. It's also too vague to plan, cost or check: nobody could tell what happens on a Monday morning.
weakExample.improved: Train 40 teachers to assess pupils' reading levels and to run a daily one-hour session with pupils grouped by level.

fields.tip: Keep to the main activities. The detailed tasks belong in your workplan. Check that every activity leads to at least one output. If one doesn't, ask whether you need it, or whether an output is missing.

sources.title: Teaching at the Right Level to improve learning
sources.organisation: J-PAL (Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab)

fields.definition: The direct, tangible results of your activities: the products, services or training your project delivers. You can count them, and they are largely within your control. Outputs are what you deliver. Outcomes are the changes that follow in people's lives.
fields.strongExample: 60 girls' clubs meeting five afternoons a week, each led by a trained young woman from the community. 1,500 girls aged 14 to 20 complete a life skills course and a vocational course of their choice.

weakExample.text: Girls are more confident and earn their own income.
weakExample.whatIsWrong: These are changes in girls' lives, so they are outcomes. Your project can't deliver them directly, because they depend on the girls themselves and on things around them, such as local jobs and family support.
weakExample.improved: 1,500 girls complete a life skills course and a vocational course, such as tailoring or hairdressing.

fields.tip: Ask of each output: can we deliver and count this ourselves? If the answer depends on other people changing what they do, it's probably an outcome. Words like 'improved', 'increased' or 'strengthened' usually signal an outcome.

sources.title: Safe spaces with vocational and life skills training for young women's economic and social empowerment in Uganda
sources.organisation: J-PAL (Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab)

fields.definition: The first changes you expect among the people you reach, as a direct result of your outputs. These are usually changes in knowledge, skills, confidence or behaviour. Your project influences them strongly, but doesn't fully control them.
fields.strongExample: Within a year of the training, more of the 1,500 market traders in the programme have introduced at least one new product and have taken out a loan to grow their business.

weakExample.text: 1,500 traders trained in a proactive business mindset.
weakExample.whatIsWrong: This is something the project delivers, so it's an output. It says nothing about what changes for the traders after the training.
weakExample.improved: Within a year, more trained traders have tried something new in their business, such as a new product or a loan to expand.

fields.tip: Write who changes and what changes, for example 'more traders introduce new products'. If you can't imagine how you'd observe or measure the change, make it more concrete.

sources.title: Theory of change in ten steps
Thinking like an entrepreneur: boosting small business growth with mindset training in Togo

fields.definition: Changes that build on the first ones and take longer to appear, often towards the end of the project or soon after. They are usually lasting changes in practice, income, wellbeing or how institutions work. Your project contributes to them, alongside other factors.
fields.strongExample: Two years after the training, participating traders earn higher monthly profits than similar traders who weren't trained, and more of them have invested in equipment or stock for their business.

weakExample.whatIsWrong: It doesn't say whose profits, compared with what, or by when, so nobody could check whether it happened.
weakExample.improved: Two years after the training, participating traders earn higher monthly profits than similar traders who weren't trained.

fields.tip: The step from short-term to medium-term outcomes is where many theories of change are weakest. Spell out why the first change should lead to the next, and what else must be true. In one evaluated training programme, women gained at first but invested less than men in their businesses, and their gains faded. Assumptions like access to money for investment are worth naming.

sources.title: Thinking like an entrepreneur: boosting small business growth with mindset training in Togo
Theory of change in ten steps

fields.definition: The lasting, long-term change you want to see for the people or place you care about. It usually takes years, goes beyond the life of your project, and depends on many actors. Your project contributes to it, but can't achieve it alone.
fields.strongExample: Small businesses run by women in the city are as profitable and long-lasting as those run by men.

weakExample.text: End poverty and empower women across Africa.
weakExample.whatIsWrong: It's far beyond what one project can meaningfully contribute to, so it can't guide your choices or show how your work adds up. Nobody could trace your contribution to it.
weakExample.improved: Women who run small businesses in the city earn as much from them as men do.

fields.tip: Many teams start here and work backwards: ask what must already be true just before this change happens, then what must be true before that. Also ask whether the change will hold for everyone. Gains that last for one group can fade for another.
